verses.text: Now Solomon decided to build a house for Yahweh’s name, and a house for his kingdom.
Solomon counted out seventy thousand men to bear burdens, eighty thousand men who were stone cutters in the mountains, and three thousand six hundred to oversee them.
Solomon sent to Huram the king of Tyre, saying, “As you dealt with David my father, and sent him cedars to build him a house in which to dwell, so deal with me.

Behold,  I am about to build a house for the name of Yahweh my God, to dedicate it to him, to burn before him incense of sweet spices, for the continual show bread, and for the burnt offerings morning and evening, on the Sabbaths, on the new moons, and on the set feasts of Yahweh our God. This is an ordinance forever to Israel.
“The house which I am building will be great; for our God is greater than all gods.
But who is able to build him a house, since heaven and the heaven of heavens can’t contain him? Who am I then, that I should build him a house, except just to burn incense before him?

“Now therefore send me a man skillful to work in gold, in silver, in brass, in iron, and in purple, crimson, and blue, and who knows how to engrave engravings, to be with the skillful men who are with me in Judah and in Jerusalem, whom David my father provided.
“Send me also cedar trees, cypress trees, and algum trees out of Lebanon; for I know that your servants know how to cut timber in Lebanon. Behold, my servants will be with your servants,
even to prepare me timber in abundance; for the house which I am about to build will be great and wonderful.

Behold, I will give to your servants, the cutters who cut timber, twenty thousand cors  of beaten wheat, twenty thousand baths  of barley, twenty thousand baths of wine, and twenty thousand baths of oil.”
Then Huram the king of Tyre answered in writing, which he sent to Solomon, “Because Yahweh loves his people, he has made you king over them.”

Huram continued, “Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, who made heaven and earth, who has given to David the king a wise son, endowed with discretion and understanding, who would build a house for Yahweh, and a house for his kingdom.
Now I have sent a skillful man, endowed with understanding, of Huram my father’s,

the son of a woman of the daughters of Dan; and his father was a man of Tyre, skillful to work in gold, in silver, in brass, in iron, in stone, in timber, and in purple, in blue, in fine linen, and in crimson, also to engrave any kind of engraving and to devise any device; that there may be a place appointed to him with your skillful men, and with the skillful men of my lord David your father.
“Now therefore the wheat the barley, the oil and the wine, which my lord has spoken of, let him send to his servants;
and we will cut wood out of Lebanon, as much as you need. We will bring it to you in floats by sea to Joppa; and you shall carry it up to Jerusalem.”
Solomon counted all the foreigners who were in the land of Israel, after the census with which David his father had counted them; and they found one hundred fifty-three thousand six hundred.
He set seventy thousand of them to bear burdens, eighty thousand who were stone cutters in the mountains, and three thousand six hundred overseers to assign the people their work.

footnotes.content: Solomon's first great decision shows the shape of his heart—not treasure, not armies, but a house for God's name. That's where he begins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Numbers here aren't just big for show; they reflect the scale of what Solomon imagines. Seventy thousand bearers, eighty thousand cutters, overseers to hold it all together—a kingdom organizing itself toward worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon honors his father's memory by appealing to David's old friendship with Huram. He doesn't presume; he asks as a son continuing what the fathers built. There's wisdom in that courtesy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Listen to what Solomon wants the Temple FOR: incense, bread, morning and evening burnt offerings, the rhythms of Sabbath and festivals. He's building a place where worship becomes the heartbeat of the nation, not an ornament.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon knows his God is greater than all gods, yet he's about to build a house. That's not contradiction—it's worship. The house can't contain Him, but it announces to the world that He is worthy of our very best effort.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here's the paradox Solomon grasps: heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain God. Yet he will build anyway. Not because a building can hold the infinite, but because a building holds the people who worship Him—and that's enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon asks for a man of many skills—gold, silver, brass, iron, purple, crimson, blue, engraving. He understands that worship requires craft, that the beauty we make speaks of the God we serve. He's not asking for merely functional; he's asking for excellent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cedar, cypress, algum from Lebanon—each wood chosen for its purpose and beauty. Solomon knows what Tyre's merchants know: that the best materials come from beyond our borders, and partnership is how great things get built.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He speaks of the house being great and wonderful. There's no shame in wanting the work of our hands to reflect something noble. When we build for God, aiming for beauty and grandeur isn't pride—it's reverence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon's payment is generous—wheat, barley, wine, oil in abundance. He knows that those who labor deserve to eat well, and that fair dealing draws out the best work from the hands of craftsmen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Huram writes back: Because Yahweh loves His people, He has made you king. That recognition from a pagan king says something—that even from a distance, God's hand is visible on a leader devoted to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Huram blesses the God of Israel—Maker of heaven and earth—and praises Solomon's wisdom. It's remarkable: a foreign king, seeing the Lord's work in another's obedience, can't help but give God glory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Huram sends his own father's craftsman—a man endowed with understanding. Notice: the best work comes from the best people. Huram gives not scraps, but his own inheritance of skill.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A son of Dan's daughter and a man of Tyre—the craftsman is himself a bridge, a child of two peoples. And his skills: gold, silver, brass, iron, stone, timber, purple, blue, linen, crimson, engraving, design. This isn't just a worker; he's an artist.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Huram agrees to Solomon's terms. Covenant-keeping is being lived out here—two kings honoring their word, each providing what was promised, each trusting the other to do the same.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The logs float by sea to Joppa, then rise inland to Jerusalem. Long before Solomon sees them shaped into beams, they're already on their journey. Faith works that way too—we say yes to what God calls, trusting He'll deliver what we need.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A hundred fifty-three thousand six hundred foreigners, counted and set apart. Solomon takes the outsiders among his people and gives them purpose. That's not just pragmatism; that's belonging.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seventy thousand bearers, eighty thousand stone cutters, three thousand six hundred overseers. Readers today hear an echo: every person has a role in building something that lasts. We're all part of something greater than ourselves, and God sees each place we fill.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
